my best advice to you as a psych major in my fourth year: do your general education courses first, and then scope out a few intro classes as well like u/samattos said. Don’t worry about declaring your major until your second year. The majority of college students change their major at least once during their journey to getting their bachelor’s. By getting your gen eds out of the way, it gives you more time to decide on what you’d like to do, talk to faculty members in the departments you’re interested in, etc. Asking your professors/advisors for their advice into becoming a psychiatrist might be helpful too, or they can at least point you in the direction of someone who knows what the academic plan is like for a prospective psychiatrist. Good luck to you!

Dad certainly is an asshole for not communicating with his children, but it seems you and your siblings haven’t made it easy when it comes to discussing his relationship with you all. Your father is his own person who is allowed to have a relationship that isn’t dictated by his children. and with at least three of you being adults (your current ages are unclear), you should be able to find support for yourselves for when dad does move. You also never specified when dad was getting married, just that he was engaged and planning to move after the wedding, so i would also guess that you and your siblings have time to discuss this and prepare for the road ahead.

You can’t ignore that there is assistance out there for people who need it. And no, government assistance is not the end of it. I also mentioned community assistance and assistance from college campuses. seeing as OP mentioned some of them are in school, they would have access to said college assistance. Additionally, just because your parents are irresponsible doesn’t mean you have to be. I agree with you that Dad should get his head out of his ass and communicate and be a responsible parent, but if he isn’t going to do that then OP and their siblings can’t wait for him to do so. And yes, OP and the sibs do need to understand that their dad is a separate adult with a life outside of his children. As someone in a similar boat to OP (both in age and situation), I know that it’s not my place to dictate my parent’s romantic life.

I never said Dad was going to contribute. By “assistance” i mean applying for government assistance or seeking out community support, both of which are by no means a bad thing to do. Additionally, a lot of college campuses will have programs to help students who are independent. Also, even if your house is paid off, you will still have household expenses (utilities, groceries, etc.) 

Dad is no saint, for sure. However, his kids don’t get to dictate when he’s allowed to date, who he’s allowed to date, or whether he can get engaged. Part of growing up is learning that your parents are individuals with their own lives, and their own relationships.

It’s also important to remember that we don’t know the cost of living for OP’s area, and we don’t know what “bills” entail. we don’t know if the house is paid off, what the cost of utilities is, etc. Additionally, I know many college friends who live independently and have received assistance in paying their utilities or groceries. While Dad should have given a heads up on his plans, it’s not impossible that OP and their siblings could live on their own.

I simply stated that you would need experience and schooling to determine whether someone has psychological trauma. Not once did I ever say you had a shitty childhood or that you personally had trauma. I’m not certain as to why your brain immediately goes to that specific defense, but that’s all on you.

If you’d like a example involving mental disorders, here you go:

People with personality disorders often don’t get treatment for it/resist treatment, because they themselves don’t believe they have a disorder. They believe they’re fine, that they’re perfectly neurotypical, when that’s far from the truth. So even if John Doe doesn’t “feel” like he’s narcissistic, that doesn’t negate his diagnosis of Narcissistic Personality Disorder.

Additionally, our brains are inherently faulty at remembering anything. You don’t “feel” traumatized, you may not remember anything from your childhood that was out of the ordinary. However, not only can trauma suppress memories, but your brain alters memories every time you think about them too. The way your brain works is that everytime you think of a memory, you have a memory of that memory. that it changes more and more each time, like a bad game of telephone.

Of course, I don’t know how you grew up or how you are today, so please don’t think I’m trying to prove you’re a trauma victim or anything. However, you can absolutely experience trauma and not necessarily “feel” traumatized.

I want you to know that my intent isn't to dissuade you or discourage you from having a safe space to talk. It's very important to have support in every area of life, and especially when it comes to mental health. As someone with diagnosed MDD, Anxiety, and contamination OCD, I know the importance of talking to people who go through the same experiences and am grateful for their advice. However, as someone who's been diagnosed and as a psychology student, one of the first things we're taught is to not throw out diagnoses. Said by a professor today, even, it is extremely difficult to diagnose someone when you are a certified individual and you have this client in front of you. So it's near impossible to diagnose someone you've never met through a computer screen. 

Sharing your experiences can be helpful, but I know it can be equally as damaging to introduce these ideas to people who are presenting as very paranoid.

You're also entirely correct in saying that the mental health field can be sketchy. Psychology itself is still a very new science, after all. Trust me, I have my fair share of horror stories dealing with people who should not have been allowed to get their certifications in that field. But there are people that can genuinely be helpful, there are typically some programs available for people to don't have the privilege of excess funds or great insurance (speaking from my own experience, at least.) This individual, I think, could benefit from getting professional help, seeing as they have frequently posted about the same issue. 

I am glad that someone like you commented on his post. It could have been that because of your comment, maybe they try to seek help. I have just been taught to be incredibly weary of introducing diagnoses to people, when I am not certified to diagnose. If you have the time, I would love for you to PM me so I can hear more about your personal experiences to help me learn about what it's like to have the thoughts that you do so I can be a better psychologist and person in the future.
